Mr. Chairman, I had intended to say a few words about the design and engraving of our postage stamps. This is a subject in which I have been interested for some time, and I spoke on one other occasion about it. Many hon. members have already referred to their commemorative suggestions for stamps, and I have criticized in some detail the various designs we now have.
I want to go back and trace the history of our stamps for a moment. In our early postage stamps, we started off in fine fashion and had some commendable stamps, not only from the philatelists' points of view but

also from the strictly art appreciation point of view. I refer particularly to the bicoloured map stamp which made Canada famous, and I also think of the early queen stamps which perhaps today do not appear to be so beautiful in the sense that we recognize, but at that time they were very good in comparison with stamps of other countries. Then we came to the stamps that were inaugurated in the 1920's, and they received very favourable comment in the postage stamp collections and from critics of those collections.
The stamp that is recognized as one of the best by collectors is the 50-cent bluenose, a blue stamp which depicted the famous Bluenose sailing ship. This stamp is in extreme demand and has been well thought of; but recently, Mr. Chairman, there has been a serious deterioration in our stamps. I do not want to dwell on the specific criticisms that have already been made here, but we know that the Canadian coronation stamp was one of the worst stamps to be issued in 1953. I perhaps am not as critical as some are about that stamp, but I feel it left much to be desired.
Then we come to the present-day situation, and the stamps are not improving. I want to make my point clear here, Mr. Chairman. I have read over the discussion in committee last year, when we had our experts from this branch of the department. I feel they are excellent men; I feel they know their job, but my criticism is that we are taking the wrong approach in our design. I think the new type of offset engraving, or whatever the method that is used, is desirable; but it is this abstract art that is creeping into our postage stamps that I object to. I feel that it is a sign again of the immaturity of Canada to try to branch out into an art field for which we are not ready. It reminds me a bit of the ballet dancers on the C.B.C. and those other related examples of new art, new-fangled art, ideas that we have.
I think the principle of giving a prize to a young Canadian artist to come up with a design is commendable; it is worth while; it should be done, but I do not think we should follow this method of abstract art in all our postage stamps. I wish to refer specifically to only one or two of the stamps that were issued. For example, our new animal stamp series is in this abstract design, and it is almost impossible to pick out the animals. In many other instances the athletes are difficult to connect with any sport. I feel that we have to get back to a simple, ordinary Canadian scene, or Canadian

animals depicted in a scene, if we want to do the best we can in this show the nations make.
Another thing that comes to my mind, Mr. Chairman, is the stamp that was issued in 1955 with respect to the boy scout jamboree.
It was a beautiful, bi-coloured, well engraved stamp, but it did not depict the activities of the boy scouts. It bore nothing of a boy scout indication. Why would it not have been possible for us to have a stamp like the one designed in New Zealand that would show our boy scouts in a camping scene, as was the case with theirs, something that would arouse the interest of the young stamp collectors in the country and at the same time be much more appreciated, I think, than abstract art on stamps? I throw that out only as a suggestion, Mr. Chairman, but it has been on my mind for some time.
If I could sum up in a brief way the points I have endeavoured to make, I might repeat that I feel Canada started off with some very commendable stamps but lately there has been a serious deterioration. We have experts in the department who are well qualified, but this matter of abstract art in our stamp designs which I think was inaugurated about 1952 is all wet. It is another indication of the immaturity of Canada.
Why would it not be possible for us to turn out a simple series of stamps depicting Canadian scenes? We could have a series of stamps running up to $1 in value each of which could depict one of the Canadian national parks or a Canadian capital city. We have splendid Canadian artists who could design stamps bearing typical Canadian scenes such as those I have mentioned. If this were done we could avoid these rather weird art expressions on stamps which no one is able to understand, explain, or appreciate. It is my hope that we can get away from the weird approach to art we have been following, so that Canada will once more be appreciated throughout the stamp world and from a collector's point of view as it once used to be.

Is
the minister not going to deal with any of the questions which have been raised and which probably come under the first item?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
That is what I intend to do, Mr. Chairman. I thought at this stage I might touch upon some of the points raised by hon. members during the course of this discussion.
At the outset may I say that I was pleased to hear so many hon. members on both sides of the house commend the officials and employees of the Post Office Department. I think we all agree that as a group postal
Supply-Post Office
employees are very good civil servants indeed, dedicated to the task of giving the best possible service to the Canadian people. I am sure that the words of appreciation expressed by hon. members in this house will be a source of great satisfaction to the employees and officials of this department, and will encourage them to continue their efforts in that direction.
I was also pleased to hear some hon. members express their satisfaction at the decentralization program which was embarked upon a few years ago and which appears to be working out very well indeed. I might say it is intended that this program be developed further with a view to bringing decision and action as close as possible to the local public.
Finally I might say that in looking over the remarks made by hon. members on Friday last, yesterday evening and this afternoon, I find a great majority of them are highly constructive and will certainly be of assistance in effecting improvements in the service.
Before I deal specifically with some of the points raised by hon. members I would like to dispel an erroneous impression which I seem to have given during the course of my remarks the other day and which resulted in the Canadian Press publishing in various newspapers across the country a news item to the effect that I had indicated the Post Office Department would have a surplus of $30 million at the end of this fiscal year. I might comment that I would like such a situation to be true, and I can think of many of the demands that have been made by hon. members that could be easily met if this were the case, but I am afraid the newspaperman who wrote that report did not analyse correctly the figures which were given.
As a matter of fact perhaps I am the one who is responsible for that. At that time, as an indication of the increased volume of business of the Post Office Department, I announced that the estimated revenue for the fiscal year ending March 31 was $169,658,000, which was an increase of approximately $11 million or 7 per cent over the previous year. I understand that in order to arrive at the figure of $30 million surplus the newspaperman who wrote this article picked up the blue book and saw that the appropriation voted by this house for the same year was $139 million, and he simply subtracted that figure from what I had indicated to be the revenue.
However, as some hon. members know, the costs of some of the activities of the Post Office Department are paid directly from the revenue of the department. If hon. members will look at section 5 and section 20 of the

Supply-Post Office
Post Office Act they will find listed the various operations which are paid under statutory authority from the revenue received. The biggest item is the remuneration of all postmasters in revenue post offices, and this alone represents an amount of $18,866,000 for the current year.
Other disbursements made from revenue receipts include expenditures for the installation of stamp vending machines, compensation to special delivery messengers, losses by fire, theft and forgery, commissions paid to foreign countries on money orders drawn on those countries, charges on parcels mailed in Canada for delivery in foreign countries, charges for the transit of Canadian mail forwarded through foreign countries and on Canadian air mail to or through foreign countries, and indemnities paid for lost insured Canadian parcels and registered letters. Disbursements for these items for the current year are estimated to be $21,500,000.
The revenue surplus would be more in the nature of $8 million, or perhaps slightly less. From that would have to be deducted an amount of $750,000 covering the increase in contracts for rural mail carriers, and an increase in rates paid to the railway companies for the transportation of mail estimated at between $850,000 and $875,000. I think by the time March 31 is reached and all bookkeeping has been completed, the net surplus of the Post Office Department will be more in the nature of $6 million.
How does that surplus compare with surpluses of previous years? Is it the largest we have had?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: It was slightly over $10 million last year, so there will be a decrease of about $4 million.

Are
the two items of expenditure to which the minister just referred contained in the estimates currently before the house?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: No. These items do not appear in the estimates, because they are made under the authority of the Post Office Act. They are met out of post office revenue. For instance, compensation to postmasters in revenue post offices is made by way of "warrants". In other words the postmaster retains his remuneration from the revenue of the post office. The estimates contain only appropriations to be voted by the house.

I am
aware of that. The Postmaster General referred to an item of freight rates which I would think should appear in the estimates.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: That will be in the supplementary estimates to be tabled by the Minister of Finance.
According to the current estimates the surplus is approximately $8,125,000.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
That will be a supplementary item. In order that hon. members may understand what would result from some of the changes they have asked for, and which may have merit, I should like to state that these things must be considered in the light of the true financial position of the department.
This brings me to a point raised by a number of hon. members, the resumption of the two deliveries a day by letter carrier service. Like many hon. members in this house I represent a constituency which is completely rural, and I do find some merit in representations that have been made that before the government returns to the two deliveries a day in the large centres it should provide a mail delivery service to those sections of the population which do not have it at the present time. I am not saying there is no merit in the representations being made for a return to two deliveries a day in certain centres, but I do believe that the present service should be extended. I consider it is the duty of the Post Office Department to expand the services to cover as large a proportion of the population as possible.
To return to the two deliveries a day would mean an increase of expenditure. When the committee on estimates was considering the estimates of the department last year two suggestions were made. One was that there should be two deliveries a day five days a week with no delivery on Saturday. The other was that there should be two deliveries a day five days a week and one delivery on Saturday. My officials believe, and I must say I share their opinion, that if two deliveries a day were instituted it would not be practical to follow the first suggestion. There are many people who remain in town on Saturday and who would like to have their mail. The accumulation of mail in the post office over the week end would be such that in many areas the delivery on Monday by letter carrier would be delayed, as there would be a much larger volume than would normally be handled.	.
For the purpose of informing the committee I may say that to implement the first suggestion it is estimated would mean an increased expenditure of $3,233,000 at the start when all the new men would be on minimum salary, and eventually the increase would amount to $3,723,000 when they had reached their maximum. In the case of two deliveries a day for five days in the week with one delivery on Saturday, it is estimated that the

increase initially would be $4,150,000, working up to $5,142,000. In addition there would be the cost of uniforms, equipment and so on.
These estimates are based on the number of calls made by the letter carriers under the old two deliveries a day system, but since that time it is well known that second class mail such as newspapers and publications has greatly increased in volume. It is problematical whether the same coverage could be given today by the letter carrier as was given in the days when two deliveries were in effect. It is practically impossible for the officials of the department to figure just what the increase would be on that score.
Now, Mr. Chairman, a certain number of members have expressed the thought that the conditions of service, the conditions of work, of postal employees are not as good as they should be, and that the salaries of postal workers generally are inadequate. Well, I can only say what was said to this committee and to the estimates committee, Mr. Chairman, and that is that these salaries, like the salaries of any other civil servants in any other government department, are determined by the civil service commission, which has the responsibility for examining salary rates in relation to rates for comparable types of work in private business and in relation to salaries paid in other government departments. They are continuously doing that work. When the department feels that adjustments should be made the commission is requested to make special surveys, but the decision is made by the civil service commission and postal employees on that score are on the same footing, shall I say, as other civil servants.
It was suggested that possibly a return to two deliveries a day would provide better working conditions and, particularly as regards letter carriers, that the volume of mail with which they are called upon to deal would be lessened if this were done. I have discussed this matter with the officers of the postal employees' association, and I have pointed out to them that if there are conditions which are beyond what should be reasonably expected, then certainly changes and improvements should be made; but that the mere act of changing over from a one delivery system to a two delivery system would not be a solution of those difficulties, and that they should be looked into and a solution found on the basis of individual cases. We have discussed a possible formula which would seem to be acceptable, and it is my intention to have the officers of the department carry on with this work.
Mr. Chairman, many hon. members have made comments regarding our postage stamps and, like the hon. member for Kootenay
Supply-Post Office
West, the hon. member for Lambton West and the hon. member for Saint John-Albert, have expressed views either in regard to our present postage stamp design or on the policy of the department respecting future issues of postage stamps. Hon. members will recall that during the sittings of the parliamentary committee on estimates and again during the discussion of the estimates of this department in the house last August, the policy of the department was outlined, and I explained that we felt that the only way to obtain good designs was to commission competent artists, particularly those interested in the subjects to be depicted on the postage stamps, and then have those designs criticized by experts; and that is precisely the policy we are following.
In connection with the recent issue of the outdoor recreation series, the hon. member for Kootenay West requested me to provide him with definite answers to the following four questions. The first was, had I ever seen anyone in Canada paddling a canoe and fishing in the manner shown on the stamp indicating a fishing expedition. I am afraid, Mr. Chairman, I must say that I have. I have myself fished in that manner, and if the hon. gentleman wants to accompany me when this session is over I will take him fishing on some of our good eastern rivers and lakes where he will sit in the bow of a canoe, with the guide in the stern paddling, so he can throw his fly or cast all over the lake.
That is right.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. member asked me, next, if I had seen any female swimming in Canada in the attitude indicated on this stamp, and in water with waves of this regular nature. Well, I am afraid I cannot pose as an authority on the attitudes of female Canadian swimmers but I noticed, on examining this stamp closely, that the person shown on the stamp was performing the crawl in the most orthodox fashion, breathing through her mouth and under her left elbow. I think it is a true form of good swimming, although it does not permit the swimmer to appear at her best.
Next the hon. member asked me if I had ever seen anyone shoot a bird in the fashion portrayed on the stamp, with a bird dog pointing as indicated. I am sorry to have to say that any dog I have owned has always been gun-shy, and I am therefore no authority on this point. The last question asked was whether I had ever seen anyone skiing on a hill with a 45 degree slope holding one pole on the snow and the other one in the air. I may say that the degree of the slope

Supply-Post Office
shown on the stamp is only 29 degrees-I checked that-but I would draw to the attention of my hon. friend a photograph cut out of the sports page of the Montreal Star of Monday, March 4, depicting Miss Josephine Frandl of Austria. The text below the picture reads:
Austrian Shows the Ladies How It's Done. Josephine Frandl of Austria was the class of the ladies' field in the Quebec Kandahar at Mt. Trem-blant. She is shown skimming down the slopes to win the slalom. She also grabbed the downhill to take the combined honours and give the Austrians a sweep of the races.
Hon. members will see that this young lady has one pole in the air and the other pole on the slope.
You are learning something.

Commonwealth of Nations-Ghana APPENDIX
Letter from the Prime Minister of Canada to the Prime Minister of Ghana:
Ottawa, February 11, 1957
My dear Prime Minister,
On the approach of the momentous day when the state of Ghana is to attain its independence, it gives me very great pleasure to convey to you the sentiments of cordial esteem which I entertain for you personally, and my desire to foster relations of friendship and good understanding between Ghana and Canada as free and equal members of the commonwealth. You may rest assured that Canada, as a senior member of the commonwealth, is particularly pleased to welcome its newest member.
I greatly regret that it is not possible for me to attend personally the important ceremonies marking the occasion when the Gold Coast joins the community of free and
independent nations; however, in order to mark this important occasion, Canada has appointed as special envoy one of our outstanding citizens, the Honourable George Prudham, member of the Queen's privy council for Canada and Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys, who, with his wife, will have the honour of representing Canada at the ceremonies of the inauguration of independence.
I know that you will give entire credence to all that Mr. Prudham may say to you, especially when he shall assure you of the sincere wish of all the people of Canada for the continuing welfare and prosperity of Ghana.
With warmest regards,
Yours sincerely,
